cards.text: Grab an apron, friend. Psalm 119 is one LONG song, and the writer never signs his name. He kicks it off with a big announcement: 'Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the Law of the LORD.'

cards.question: The writer says the blessed also keep God's testimonies. How much of themselves do they put into seeking Him?
According to the writer, the blessed people who walk in God's ways do no iniquity.

cards.text: Then he turns and talks straight to God: 'You have ordained Your precepts, that we should keep them diligently.' Then he takes a good look at his own life.

cards.question: After saying God's precepts should be kept diligently, what does the writer wish about his own ways?

answers.text: That they were committed to keeping God's statutes
That they were easier than other people's ways
That nobody would ever look at them closely

cards.question: The writer says that if his ways were committed to God's statutes, he would not be ashamed when he considers all God's commandments.

cards.text: That wish is me holding my batch up next to the photo on the cookie box going, 'Oh, if ONLY.' Still, he promises to praise God with an upright heart when he learns His righteous judgments.

cards.question: The writer promises God, 'I will keep Your statutes.' What does he ask God in the very same breath?

answers.text: To give him a long life

cards.text: New stretch, and he opens it with a question: 'How can a young man keep his way pure?'

cards.question: The writer's answer: a young man keeps his way pure by guarding it according to God's ___.

cards.text: He's sought God with all his heart, and he STILL asks God not to let him stray from His commandments. Honest man, because I cross this bakery for ONE chocolate chip and come back holding the whole bag.

cards.question: The writer tells God, 'I have hidden Your word in my heart.' Why does he say he did it?

answers.text: So he might not sin against God
So no one could take it from him
So he could win every argument

cards.text: Now he flips it around and blesses God Himself: 'Blessed are You, O LORD.'

cards.question: Right after saying 'Blessed are You, O LORD,' what does the writer ask God to do?

cards.text: He isn't keeping any of it quiet, either: with his lips he proclaims all the judgments of God's mouth. Mags would LOVE this guy.

cards.question: The writer rejoices in the way of God's testimonies as much as in all ___.

cards.text: ALL riches! Friend, Mother Miller bought me out of a bin for a quarter, so riches is not my area of expertise. He says he'll meditate on God's precepts and regard His ways.

cards.question: The writer says God's statutes are a chore he just puts up with.

cards.text: He delights in them, and he promises: 'I will not forget Your word.' Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer full of instruction manuals NOBODY remembered, so that one hits me right in the apron.
Next stretch, and the writer calls himself God's servant. He asks, 'Deal bountifully with Your servant.'

cards.question: The writer asks God to deal bountifully with him. What does he say it's for?

answers.text: So he may live and keep God's word
So he may rule over his enemies
So he may build a great house

cards.text: Then comes a prayer I need every single morning: 'Open my eyes.'

cards.question: When God opens his eyes, what does the writer want to see?

answers.text: The road back to his home

cards.text: He calls himself a stranger on the earth. That's your first day at a new job: you don't know where ANYTHING is, and you need somebody to show you.

cards.question: Because he's a stranger on the earth, the writer asks God not to hide His ___ from him.
The writer says his soul longs for God's judgments only every now and then.

cards.text: At ALL times! That's me pressed up against the oven window watching a batch, except he NEVER steps back.

cards.question: The writer says God rebukes the arrogant, the cursed who stray from His commandments.

cards.text: Then he asks God to take something off his shoulders: his scorn and contempt.

cards.question: Why does the writer ask God to remove his scorn and contempt?

answers.text: He comes from a respected family

cards.text: Then rulers sit and slander him. That's the worst group chat in the world, and he's the only topic.

cards.question: While rulers sit and slander him, what does God's servant do?

answers.text: He hides away in the hills

cards.question: The writer says God's testimonies are his ___, and they are his ___.

cards.text: His delight AND his counselors! We'll leave it here for now, friend, but trust me, this psalm is far from done.

findings.problem: The right answer 'All their heart' sounds biblical, while 'Half their attention' and 'Their spare time' sound modern and close to silly. The baker can pick the right answer from its tone alone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: 'Still, he promises...' frames verse 7 as a contrast with verses 5-6. The text sets the lines side by side and never says how they connect.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: 'He's sought God with all his heart, and he STILL asks...' frames the two halves of verse 10 as a contrast. The text only puts them side by side.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't match the action in the verse. Verse 10 is about straying from God's commandments. Crossing the bakery for one chocolate chip and coming back with the whole bag is about taking too much, not wandering off course.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Nothing before this card points to 'riches' over 'feasts' or 'harvests'. The blank asks the baker to guess the wording of the line, so it can only be answered by luck.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'ALL riches!', the Mother Miller line, and the line about meditating on God's precepts. Only the opening card may have three.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: 'Because he's a stranger on the earth, the writer asks...' adds a reason. Verse 19 puts the two statements side by side with a semicolon and never says one causes the other.

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: Verse 23 says 'Though rulers sit and slander me.' The card turns this into a narrated event ('Then rulers sit and slander him'). It drops 'though' and adds a time sequence the text doesn't give.
